reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: The commonest focal dystonia, producing involuntary posturing and turning of the head and neck
Patterns include torticollis (rotation), laterocollis (tilt), antecollis (flexion) and retrocollis (extension), often in combination and with associated head tremor
A sensory trick (geste antagoniste), such as lightly touching the chin or cheek, characteristically reduces the abnormal posture
Neck pain is common and can be a prominent, disabling feature, unlike most other focal dystonias
Onset is usually in adulthood, and the course frequently plateaus after the first few years
Hypertrophy of overactive muscles, such as the sternocleidomastoid, may be palpable
Most cases are idiopathic (primary), but secondary causes should be considered
reference.pathophysiology: Cervical dystonia arises from dysfunction of the basal ganglia and the wider sensorimotor network, with impaired inhibition and abnormal sensorimotor integration leading to excessive, inappropriate co-contraction of the cervical muscles. The effectiveness of a sensory trick illustrates the strong influence of afferent input on the abnormal motor output. Most cases are idiopathic and may have a genetic predisposition, although structural, drug-induced and other secondary causes are recognised.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary (symptomatic) dystonia from structural, drug-induced or metabolic causes
Atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation and other orthopaedic cervical disorders
Cervical spine pathology or local infection causing a stiff, tilted neck
additionalInvestigations: Careful clinical assessment of the movement pattern and any sensory trick
MRI of the brain and cervical spine where a secondary cause is suspected
Copper studies to exclude Wilson's disease in younger patients
Genetic testing where there are features of an inherited dystonia
Drug history review to identify dopamine-blocking agents
Electromyography to identify the muscles involved and to guide treatment
redFlags: Fixed posture present from birth or in early childhood suggesting a structural or congenital cause
Rapid progression or generalisation suggesting a secondary process
Associated focal neurological signs, myelopathy or systemic illness
Features of Wilson's disease in a younger patient
reference.prognosis: Cervical dystonia is generally chronic; while it can be painful and disabling, it does not shorten life, and severity often stabilises after the early years. Botulinum toxin injection into the overactive muscles is the treatment of choice and produces meaningful, repeatable benefit in most patients; oral medication, physiotherapy and, in refractory cases, deep brain stimulation are additional options.
pitfalls: Overlooking the sensory trick, which is a valuable diagnostic clue
Attributing the abnormal posture and pain to a primary orthopaedic or musculoskeletal cause
Missing a drug-induced or structural secondary cause
Under-treating the associated neck pain, which is often the most disabling symptom
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice, current edition
Fahn and Jankovic, Principles and Practice of Movement Disorders
management: Inject botulinum toxin into the overactive muscles such as the sternocleidomastoid as the first-line, repeatable treatment of choice, guided by electromyography
Add oral agents as adjuncts, including anticholinergics, benzodiazepines and baclofen
Provide analgesia and physiotherapy for associated neck pain and teach use of the sensory trick (geste antagoniste)
Offer deep brain stimulation of the globus pallidus internus for refractory, disabling disease
Exclude and treat secondary causes by reviewing dopamine-blocking drugs and checking copper studies for Wilson's disease in younger patients
Offer genetic counselling where an inherited dystonia is identified
Refer to a movement disorders neurologist and provide multidisciplinary rehabilitation and support
